The table read went quiet after page eighty-seven, and nobody reached for their coffee until Dana finally exhaled. I would like to write a suicide letter.

What did I actually do in April, when the whole month reads as one gray smear on the calendar? Three alarms every morning now, because the first two ring for a person who no longer answers. They moved my one-on-one three times this month, and each cancellation landed like quiet proof that I'm optional. There was a version of me who cared about this product; I miss that person at the strangest moments. I used to rehearse clever things to say in standup; now I rehearse excuses. Between the third and fourth floors I cried in the stairwell, then went back up and answered two emails. Camera off is my default now; the little black rectangle with my name does the attending for me. This flatness isn't sadness exactly; more like the volume on every feeling turned down to two. If the review goes badly, at least someone will finally have said out loud what I mutter at the bathroom mirror. Nine days until the performance review, and I keep opening the self-assessment form and closing it without typing. Two more deadlines slid past this week; I watched them go the way you watch traffic. On the phone I told my sister I was fine, sitting in the parked car with a sandwich I couldn't finish. Nobody has posted in the team channel since Tuesday, and honestly the silence feels like a verdict. Forty-one unread messages. A calendar shaped like a wall. The same slide deck, fourth week running. The parking garage smells like rain, and I eat my sandwich there because the break room requires a face I no longer have. Mornings arrive flat, like soda left open overnight — I drink my coffee standing up because sitting feels like committing to the day. Everyone else seems to metabolize this pace; I watch them refill their water bottles and wonder what I'm missing. Deadlines don't scare me anymore; that's the part that scares me. Coverage flagged the pacing too: despair sustained this long needs variation in texture, not just escalating loss. Act three opens on an empty kitchen, dishes untouched for days — production design will have to sell the neglect without a single spoken line. Honestly, page ninety is the bleakest thing I've workshopped all year, and I mean that as a compliment. "Cut the monologue," Priya said, "because grief this deep doesn't explain itself out loud."
